findings.topic: still air in low gravity confines smoke near the source
findings.claim: The report estimates that with zero flow in microgravity, transport is by molecular diffusion and thermal expansion: in 60 seconds the gases would diffuse on the order of 4 cm, which (assuming a cubical geometry) confines the smoke to about 64 cm3 instead of diluting it in the 6000 cm3 piston, so that, if the same number of particles is generated, the initial concentration is on the order of 50 times higher than with flow.
findings.quote: The transport for the zero-flow case in μ-g is controlled by molecular diffusion and thermal expansion. Over a period of 60 seconds, the gases would diffuse a distance on the order of 4 cm. Assuming a cubical geometry this would correspond to the smoke being confined to a volume of about 64 cm3 rather than being diluted in the 6000 cm3 piston. If the same number of particles is generated as for the flow case, the initial concentration will be on the order of 50 times higher for the zero-flow case.

findings.topic: three mechanisms behind larger microgravity smoke
findings.claim: The simulations point to three mechanisms that separate microgravity from Earth-gravity smoke: different recirculation geometries and volumes, particle settling removing large particles on Earth, and buoyant convection carrying condensable species toward cool surfaces.
findings.quote: three primary mechanisms that differentiate the microgravity and Earth gravity smoke: (1) different re- circulation geometries and volumes modify the time-temperature-concentration history of the aerosol in regions of high temperature and high vapor mass fraction; (2) particle settling eliminates large particles from Earth gravity smoke, which reduces the maximum particle size and modifies aerosol development by changing coagulation and condensation rates of the remaining particles; (3) buoyant convection can transport condensible species toward relatively cool surfaces, increasing vapor-to-particle conversion.

In these situations, microgravity and Earth gravity smoke are hypothesized to be more similar.

findings.topic: Why carbon dioxide can behave differently without buoyancy
findings.claim: The FLEX test plan explains that without buoyantly-driven convective flows, radiative losses can become a significant fraction of the heat loss from the reaction zone, and that when a thermally participating gas such as CO2 limits radiative exchange between flame and ambient, temperatures near the fuel source will increase.
findings.quote: In the absence of buoyantly-driven convective flows, however, radiative losses from the flame can become a significant fraction of the total heat loss from the reaction zone. When radiative exchanges between the flame and the ambient are limited by the presence of a thermally participating gas, such as CO2 , temperatures in the proximity of the fuel source will increase.

findings.topic: Fuel keeps reacting after the visible flame is gone
findings.claim: In FLEX, large alkane droplets burned briefly with a typical hot flame that extinguished when radiative loss lowered the flame temperature; after that the droplet continued to vaporize at the same rate for an extended period and then suddenly stopped at a finite size, with a large vapor cloud forming; this vaporization is supported by a lower-temperature cool flame that forms after visible flame extinction.
findings.quote: Recent spaceflight experiments (FLEX) involving single alkane droplets burning in a quiescent ambient uncovered unexplained and unexpected behavior. For the large alkane droplets, after ignition the droplet burns for a short time with a typical hot flame. As expected, the hot flame extinguished when the radiative loss reduced the flame temperature below a critical value. Inexplicably after hot flame extinction, however, the droplet continued to vaporize at the same rate for an extended period and then suddenly stopped vaporizing at a finite droplet size. The plateau in vaporization occurred coincident with the formation of a large vapor cloud. This vaporization, we now know, is supported by a lower-temperature cool flame that forms after visible flame extinction.

findings.topic: Post-flame vaporization nearly as fast as burning (heptane in cabin air)
findings.claim: In FLEX test 035 (free-floating heptane droplet, cabin air, 1.0 atm), after the visible flame extinguished the droplet vaporized very vigorously at a rate only slightly lower than the burning rate constant before extinction, then the rate plateaued as a very large vapor cloud formed; the report calls this indicative of cool flame burning and extinction.
findings.quote: Figure 39.—Test FLEX−035. Free-floating heptane droplet in a cabin air (0.21/0.79 O2/N2), 1.0-atm ambient environment. The droplet remained in the High-Bit-Depth Multispectral (HiBMs) field of view (FOV) for the entire test including a long time after the visible flame extinguished. The flame oscillated before the visible flame extinguished, and this was apparent in both the Low Light Level Ultra-Violet (LLUV) and color camera. After the flame extinguished, the droplet vaporized very vigorously with droplet-diameter-squared versus time behavior that was nearly perfectly linear. The vaporization rate was only slightly lower than the burning rate constant before the flame extinguished. The droplet vaporization rate then plateaued coincident with the formation of a very large vapor cloud. This behavior is indicative of cool flame burning and extinction.

The influence of CO2 concentration in the ambient is summarized in Figure 6. An increase 5 in the CO2 concentration in the ambient readily triggered the “Cool flame” combustion. The “Cool Flame” behavior can not only be triggered by radiative heat loss but rather any enhanced heat loss mechanism.

findings.topic: Model: flash re-ignition after about 18 s of cool flame
findings.claim: A two-dimensional simulation using a gaseous n-heptane source in zero gravity predicts that in air at <=2 mm/s, with fuel injection velocity 1 cm/s, a growing spherical flame radiatively extinguishes at about 1200 K, transitions to a roughly 700 K cool-flame regime, and after about 18 s undergoes flash re-ignition followed by extinction of the re-ignited flame.
findings.quote: In a near-quiescent air environment (< or = 2 mm/s), with a sufficiently large fuel injection velocity (1 cm/s), a growing spherical diffusion flame extinguishes at ≈1200 K due to radiative heat losses. This is typically followed by a transition to the low-temperature (cool-flame) regime with a reaction zone (at ≈700 K) in close proximity to the fuel source. The 'cool flame' regime is formed due to the negative temperature coefficient in the low-temperature chemistry. After a relatively long period (≈18 s) of the cool flame regime, a flash re-ignition occurs, associated with flame-edge propagation and subsequent extinction of the re-ignited flame.

findings.topic: Visible flame extinguished after 3 mm/s droplet translation stopped
findings.claim: In FLEX test 064 a fiber-supported heptane droplet in 0.18/0.82 O2/N2 at 1.0 atm was translated at 3 mm/s for about 4 s: during translation the leading edge of the flame was bright and the trailing edge much dimmer; after translation stopped the flame extinguished and the droplet vaporized significantly, behavior the report calls indicative of cool flame burning and extinction.
findings.quote: Figure 68.—Test FLEX−064. Fiber-supported heptane droplet translating 3 mm/s (for approximately 4 s) and burning in a 0.18/0.82 O2/N2, 1.0-atm ambient environment. The droplet had moderate transverse oscillations and remained within the High-Bit-Depth Multispectral (HiBMs) field of view (FOV) for the entire test. The flame grew and became dim blue. During translation, the leading edge of the flame was bright and the fiber glowed brightly. The trailing edge of the flame was much dimmer and the fiber did not glow. After the translation stopped, the flame extinguished and the droplet vaporized significantly. A small disruption very late in the droplet lifetime left a small residual droplet on the fiber. The behavior after the visible flame extinguished is indicative of cool flame burning and extinction.

findings.topic: Precursor tests: carbon dioxide at fixed 21% oxygen barely changed methanol extinction
findings.claim: In precursor microgravity experiments (before the ISS runs) with 1.25 to 1.72 mm methanol droplets at one atmosphere and oxygen fixed at 21%, the extinction diameter grew with initial droplet diameter, while increasing the carbon dioxide concentration led only to a slight decrease in the extinction diameter.
findings.quote: Diffusive extinction of methanol droplets with initial diameters between 1.25 mm and 1.72 mm, burning in a quiescent microgravity environment at one atmosphere pressure, was obtained experimentally for varying levels of ambient carbon-dioxide concentrations with a fixed oxygen concentration of 21% and a balance of nitrogen. These experiments serve as precursors to those which are beginning to be performed on the International Space Station and are motivated by the need to understand the effectiveness of carbon-dioxide as a fire suppressant in low-gravity environments. In these experiments, the flame standoff distance, droplet diameter, and flame radiation are measured as functions of time. The results show that the droplet extinction diameter depends on both the initial droplet diameter and the ambient concentration of carbon dioxide. Increasing the initial droplet diameter leads to an increased extinction diameter, while increasing the carbon-dioxide concentration leads to a slight decrease in the extinction diameter.

findings.quote: Figure 8 shows the burning behavior for a single droplet and a binary array (L ≈ 3 mm) in a 0.15 oxygen mole fraction (balance nitrogen), 190 mmHg ambient. There are several noteworthy features of the single droplet burning behavior. First, this ambient condition was not ﬂammable in normal gravity. In fact, in this ambient oxygen mole fraction, droplets of this size could not sustain a ﬂame in normal gravity at pressures up to 760 mmHg. Figure 8 also shows that while the single droplet burned to completion, the ﬂame surrounding the array extinguished approximately one second after the igniter withdrew.

findings.topic: Cameras saw nothing during the cool flame; radiometers did
findings.claim: During the second, cool-flame stage of an n-decane droplet burn, neither the color camera nor the UV camera was sensitive enough to register any flame image, while both the broadband and narrowband radiometers registered continued radiative heat loss from the droplet, indicating active chemical heat release.
findings.quote: The second-stage combustion termed "cool flame" zone starts immediately following hot-flame extinction. As in the hot-flame region the square of the droplet diameter decreases linearly with time in the cool-flame region, but at a slightly slower rate. Both the color camera and the UV-camera are not sensitive enough to register any flame images during this period. Both the broadband and narrowband radiometers, however, register continued radiative heat loss from the droplet indicating active chemical heat release. The end of "cool flame" combustion is clearly marked by the rapid drop in the narrowband radiometer output. Following cool flame extinction the droplet simply evaporates in the hot environment and the radiative loss measurements decay to zero values without any further abrupt changes.

findings.topic: 75% helium: hot flame died in a fraction of a second, brief cool flame followed
findings.claim: In test R707 of the paper's n-octane series, at 75% helium dilution and initial diameter 2.49 mm, the hot flame died within a fraction of a second and a short cool flame followed. The entire process was transient and quasi-steady burning was not achieved.
findings.quote: When helium dilution was increased to 75% by volume in test R707 for D0 of 2.49 mm first stage burning is almost eliminated (see, Fig. (2d)). The hot flame that formed during the ignition dies within a fraction of a second and the cool flame burning commences immediately which also ends quickly leaving the droplet to evaporate. The high thermal conductivity of helium leads to large heat loss from the flame zone and as a consequence the flame temperature rapidly decreases leading to cool flame extinction. The entire process was transient and quasi- steady burning was not achieved.

findings.topic: Model: hot, warm and cool flame temperatures at elevated pressure
findings.claim: The abstract reports simulations of isolated n-alkane droplets at elevated pressure in helium-substituted air. It predicts roughly 1500 K hot, 970 K warm and 765 K cool stages, with all three first appearing near 20% helium substitution and their duration strongly dependent on substitution from 20% to 60%. Above 60%, hot-flame extinction is followed only by the lower-temperature cool stage.
findings.quote: Transient, isolated n-alkane droplet combustion is simulated at elevated pressure for helium-diluent substituted-air mixtures. We report the presence of unique quasi-steady, three-stage burning behavior of large sphero-symmetric n-alkane droplets at these elevated pressures and helium substituted ambient fractions. Upon initiation of reaction, hot-flame diffusive burning of large droplets is initiated that radiatively extinguishes to establish cool flame burning conditions in nitrogen/oxygen "air" at atmospheric and elevated pressures. However, at elevated pressure and moderate helium substitution for nitrogen ( X He > 20%), the initiated cool flame burning proceeds through two distinct, quasi-steady-state, cool flame burning conditions. The classical "Hot flame " ( ∼1500 K) radiatively extinguishes into a "Warm flame " burning mode at a moderate maximum reaction zone temperature ( ∼ 970 K), followed by a transition to a lower temperature ( ∼765 K), quasi-steady "Cool flame " burning condition. The reaction zone ("flame") temperatures are associated with distinctly different yields in intermediate reaction products within the reaction zones and surrounding near-field, and the flame-standoff ratios characterizing each burning mode progressively decrease. The presence of all three stages first appears with helium substitution near 20%, and the duration of each stage is observed to be strongly dependent on helium substitutions level between 20-60%. For helium substitution greater than 60%, the hot flame extinction is followed by only the lower temperature cool flame burning mode.

findings.topic: radiation-dominated smoke point
findings.claim: The SPICE final report states that results from the Laminar Soot Processes experiment showed that removing buoyancy can make the smoke point dominated by radiative heat losses at low flame velocity, with the flame extinguishing at its tip and letting soot escape.
findings.quote: Results from an MSL-1 combustion project, the Laminar Soot Processes (LSP), revealed that the smoke height phenomenon in microgravity can be substantially different form that seen in normal gravity. The removal of buoyancy induced acceleration can cause the smoke point phenomenon to be dominated by radiative heat losses for conditions of low overall flame velocity. Under these conditions the flame extinguishes at the flame tip allowing soot to be emitted. In spite of this effect, it is still possible to have flames that either emit soot along all stream lines or do not emit soot anywhere, for conditions where radiation losses do not dominate.

findings.topic: soot release collapsed the airflow
findings.claim: After SLICE tests run above the smoke point with soot streaming from the flame, the reference air velocity at maximum fan voltage fell to one fifth of its previous value, from ~43 cm/s to ~9 cm/s.
findings.quote: The fan calibration at the end of this day’s session revealed a dramatic drop in the coflow where Stocker had guided Petit through test conditions that exceeded the smoke point, i.e., where soot was streaming out of the flame. In contrast, the SPICE procedure was to reach and identify the smoke point and then reduce the flow to avoid the soot release. With the fan at the maximum voltage during the calibration, the reference velocity dropped to one fifth of what it had been at the end of the previous session (on March 19), i.e., from ~43 cm/s to ~9 cm/s.

findings.topic: three mechanisms behind the size difference
findings.claim: The PSI-115 final report names three mechanisms that differentiate microgravity and Earth-gravity smoke: different recirculation geometries, particle settling that removes large particles on Earth, and buoyant convection carrying condensable species toward cool surfaces.
findings.quote: Results exhibit three primary mechanisms that differentiate the microgravity and Earth gravity smoke: (1) different re- circulation geometries and volumes modify the time-temperature-concentration history of the aerosol in regions of high temperature and high vapor mass fraction; (2) particle settling eliminates large particles from Earth gravity smoke, which reduces the maximum particle size and modifies aerosol development by changing coagulation and condensation rates of the remaining particles; (3) buoyant convection can transport condensible species toward relatively cool surfaces, increasing vapor-to-particle conversion. Each of these factors tend to increase the size of particles in microgravity relative to Earth gravity. How- ever, each of these factors is also highly material- and geometry-dependent: (1) the wake dynamic becomes unimportant if nucleation occurs far downstream of the wake, or if there is a time dependent flow without a stable recirculation region; (2) particle settling is irrelevant if the condensing species forms particles that are too small to settle (the DBP considered in this work forms large particles); (3) if smoke is produced in an open environment, there may not be cool surfaces nearby to increase nucleation rates. In these situations, microgravity and Earth gravity smoke are hypothesized to be more similar.

findings.topic: what the data set contains
findings.claim: The PSI-142 record describes three numerical schemes for comparing oxygen effects on cool-flame extinction: n-heptane/air spark-assisted propagation, freely propagating DME flames, and elevated-pressure DME/air burning limits.
findings.quote: Using the experimental conditions of FLEX flight, a comparative studies of the oxygen concentration effects on the extinction limits of cool flames was conducted using three different numerical modeling schemes, (a) spark-assisted flame propagation of a n-heptane/air mixture, (b) one dimensional freely-propagating dimethyl ether (DME) flames using an arc-length continuation method and (c) simulated cool flame regimes and burning limits at elevated pressure (up to 20\u202fatm) using DME/air mixtures.

The spectral emissivity for PMMA was calculated and incorporated into the calibration of the camera.Surface temperatures from the IR camera are compared to results from thermocouples embedded in the surface of the fuel. findings.claim: A new normal-gravity upward flame spread test method extrapolates the linear blowoff boundary to the zero stretch limit to resolve microgravity flammability limits.
